stories.title: Nouriel Roubini: the world is in turmoil, so why is the global economy still chugging along?
points: After the 2025 ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs and this year’s Iran War, the biggest energy shock since the 1970s, IMF data still show global growth at 3.5% in 2025, the same as 2024, with lower inflation.

Four props, he argues: markets forced a tariff retreat (from 21.5% in April 2025 to 9.6% now) and a fragile Iran ceasefire; new energy sources and China’s oil reserves cushioned the shock; policy easing, then tightening; and, above all, the AI investment boom.
Risks: oil back above $100, a constrained Strait of Hormuz, Taiwan and Russia–Ukraine, populist elections, heavy debt and a frothy AI boom. He still sees the positive scenario as more likely.
stories.why: Jobs, savings and loan rates on both sides of the world ride on whether this resilience holds, and much of it now hinges on AI.
stories.other: If AI spending is the main prop, is the resilience real or borrowed from a boom that could deflate? Growth forecasts made in wartime can also age fast.

stories.title: Mint Explainer: Why is Elon Musk’s Starlink at war with Indian telecom giants?
points: On Wednesday Musk posted that unnamed Indian ‘oligarchs’ were blocking Starlink’s launch to keep a ‘monopolistic chokehold’; on Thursday the government called any suggestion of bias ‘baseless and misconceived’, citing security assessments under way.

Starlink won its licence in June 2025, after OneWeb and Jio Satellite in 2022; more than four years after the first licence, commercial launches for all players remain stalled over security and data-sovereignty concerns.

Jio wanted satellite spectrum auctioned; in September 2026 the telecom department chose administrative allocation with a 5% charge on adjusted gross revenue, still awaiting cabinet approval. Ironically, Airtel and Jio have both signed pacts with SpaceX to offer Starlink.
stories.why: Satellite internet can reach places towers and fibre don’t; who gets to sell it, and on what terms, shapes India’s connectivity.
stories.other: Is this protectionism, or a fair wait for security checks on foreign-run satellites carrying Indian data? Musk named no one, and his rivals are also his Indian partners.

stories.title: 20,000-plus people shift as IT firms buy GCCs and captive tech carve-outs
points: More than 20,000 employees moved from GCCs, enterprise IT units and product operations to IT services firms in the past 12 months; analyst Pareekh Jain expects similar numbers in the next 12.

TCS took over Best Buy’s India GCC; HCLTech bought Guardian Life’s India operations for $10.5 million (nearly 2,000 staff); Wipro paid $386 million for Olam’s Mindsprint (3,200+ staff), tied to an eight-year deal expected to bring over $1 billion.
HFS’s Achyuta Ghosh says about 10% of mature GCCs could be fully or partly transferred in two to three years, mostly operations-heavy, labour-intensive centres; deals usually involve 500–3,000 staff.
stories.why: In a low-growth market, IT firms are buying growth with long contracts attached, and thousands of staff are changing employers.
stories.other: Is this a vote of confidence in IT firms, or a sign that many GCCs never reached scale? And how do transferred staff fare once AI-led productivity is priced into the contract?

stories.title: India’s aspirational middle class gives it a demographic edge, says Verlinvest CEO Roberto Italia
points: Verlinvest plans to invest €1 billion in India over the next five years, with opportunities in health, fitness and digital content.

CEO Roberto Italia, 60, manages €2 billion for Belgian families who are long-standing AB InBev shareholders; their 31-year-old evergreen capital has backed Vita Coco, Oatly, Chewy, Epigamia, Juicy Chemistry and Wakefit.

He says a large share of Indians are becoming, or aim to become, middle class and are willing to spend; even amid AI job fears, India’s young population stays a strategic asset. He likens Mumbai to 1990s New York.
stories.why: Patient global capital is betting on India’s spending power, which feeds the brands, startups and jobs behind it.
stories.other: A ‘demographic edge’ is a compelling story, and investors pitch their own bets. Will jobs and incomes keep pace with the aspirations?

stories.title: What do you gift the Swiss President? PM Modi chose three Indian cheeses
points: On Monday, 5 October, in New Delhi, PM Narendra Modi gave Swiss President Guy Parmelin three award-winning Indian cheeses: Gulmarg, Konark and Yeoor.
Parmelin is in India on a three-day state visit; the gift was presented as a showcase of India’s growing cheesemaking tradition, with a nod to Switzerland’s own fame for cheese.
stories.why: Soft power on a plate: India offering its own craft to the home of cheese.
stories.other: A gift is a gesture, not a market. Will Indian artisan cheese find buyers abroad beyond the diplomatic table?

stories.title: ‘Switzerland has spoken’: will UBS leave?
points: Three and a half years after its state-orchestrated rescue of Credit Suisse, UBS faces a Swiss proposal, backed last month by parliament’s upper house, to hold an extra $16bn of capital; the lower house still has to vote.

Its options: stay and pay (analysts put the real shortfall at $6bn–8bn), split off the international arm, sell or shrink the US business, merge with a foreign bank, or leave Switzerland, which Morgan Stanley says could bring an exit tax of up to $10bn.

Top-10 shareholder Artisan Partners has urged a move; finance minister Karin Keller-Sutter says leaving would be ‘much more expensive and legally very complex’. A senior UBS employee says staying and adapting is most likely.
stories.why: After Credit Suisse, Switzerland is choosing safety over its biggest bank’s growth, and banks and investors everywhere are watching.
stories.other: Is this overcaution that could push a national champion abroad, or a fair price for a bank whose balance sheet is bigger than the Swiss economy? Rivals, for their part, welcome a competitor forced to hold more capital.

stories.title: Devina Mehra: the art of storytelling can turn into an investment pitfall, even for veterans
points: We respond to stories, not statistics. A fund manager’s tale of great brands and endless growth persuades people, but the market doesn’t care how well a story is told.
Valuations assume earnings grow forever, yet of 4,000-plus stocks listed in India only 17 have grown profit every year for even a decade: just 0.4%.
Warren Buffett held his Coca-Cola story too long: from its 1998 high Coke has returned about 4x with dividends, against 6x for Pepsi and 11x for the S&P 500.
stories.why: Before you buy, test the story behind the stock and imagine other endings.
stories.other: Conviction also stops investors panic-selling, and long holds of great companies have built fortunes. Where does a sound thesis end and a story begin?
